title: Proceedings of the CSCW 2026 Workshop on Women's Health as Cooperative Work: Participatory AI Across Care, Community, and Policy
comment: Proceedings index for the CSCW 2026 workshop held on October 11, 2026. Editor: Sherilyn Francis. Individual papers are submitted separately to arXiv
summary:
This submission indexes contributions to the CSCW 2026 workshop, "Women's Health as Cooperative Work: Participatory AI Across Care, Community, and Policy," held on October 11, 2026. The workshop examines women's health as cooperative work spanning patients, caregivers, clinicians, communities, institutions, and digital technologies. Contributions explore participatory AI, coordination breakdowns, the distribution of care labor, governance, decision-making authority, and accountability across care, community, and policy contexts.
  The index provides paper titles, authors, affiliations, thematic areas, and unique report numbers to support discovery of the corresponding individual arXiv submissions.
  The workshop proposal is separately published under DOI 10.1145/3785651.3818821.

AI.tldr: This submission is an index of contributions to a CSCW 2026 workshop on women's health as cooperative work. It organizes papers by titles, authors, affiliations, themes, and report identifiers, directing readers to the corresponding arXiv submissions rather than presenting a standalone empirical study.
AI.motivation: The index is motivated by the need to make a diverse set of workshop contributions discoverable and to frame women's health as distributed cooperative work involving patients, caregivers, clinicians, communities, institutions, and technologies. It foregrounds challenges involving coordination, care labor, governance, decision authority, and accountability.
AI.method: The submission uses an indexing and bibliographic organization approach. It catalogs workshop papers and associated metadata, including thematic areas and unique report numbers, while pointing readers to individual arXiv records. The abstract does not specify empirical data collection, analysis procedures, or an AI system evaluation.
AI.result: The stated output is a structured discovery resource for the workshop contributions. The abstract does not report experimental findings, quantitative results, qualitative themes, or performance metrics; those results would need to be obtained from the linked individual submissions.
AI.conclusion: The submission functions primarily as a bibliographic gateway and conceptual overview of a participatory-AI workshop. Its central contribution is to organize and contextualize research on women's health as cooperative work across care, community, and policy settings, rather than to establish independent research conclusions.

title: From Benchmarks to Behaviors: A Framework for Auditing AI Agents
summary: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate access to information. Their behavior depends on tools, instructions, and user memories that are often difficult for researchers to observe or control. Here, I introduce TRACE (Transparent Research on Agent Contexts and Environments), a framework for systematically auditing how these components shape AI agent behavior. Built on an open-source agent harness, TRACE enables controlled manipulation of system components. It also records inputs, outputs, and task execution for downstream analysis. I demonstrate this framework through an experiment examining how user memories influence source selection when agents answer questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections. I find that memories expressing explicit preference for a publisher increase its inclusion among the first three cited sources in a response by 33-39 percentage points. Memories identifying the user as a Republican or expressing distrust of mainstream media shift citations rightward. That same media distrust memory also increases citation of sources expressing misinformation or conspiracy theories by 6.3 percentage points, with substantial variation across models. These findings demonstrate that concise user memories can alter source selection in consequential settings, even when questions and search results remain fixed. TRACE extends algorithm auditing to agent harnesses, providing a transparent way to study agent behaviors that benchmarks or commercial interfaces may struggle to isolate.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TRACE, a framework for auditing how agent context and environment components influence generative AI behavior.
AI.motivation: To make hidden or difficult-to-control agent components, such as tools, instructions, and user memories, observable and systematically testable.
AI.method: TRACE uses an open-source agent harness to manipulate system components under controlled conditions and records inputs, outputs, and task execution for analysis.
AI.result: The study finds that user memories can substantially change source selection even when the question and search results are fixed, with effects varying across models.
AI.conclusion: TRACE broadens algorithm auditing to agent harnesses and enables more transparent analysis than standard benchmarks or commercial interfaces alone.

title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task
summary: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order. Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no increase in reported mental demand. Our findings show that people can recover what the system left implicit and that pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under the constraints of a changing world.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that users can effectively interpret deliberately incomplete alerts from an assistive system when the system accounts for their prior knowledge. Compared with fully explicit alerts, pragmatic alerts supported faster monitoring, improved problem detection, and were judged more helpful without increasing reported mental demand.
AI.motivation: Assistive systems often communicate every detail, including information users already know. This can waste limited attention and delay responses to new or critical developments. The study investigates whether people can infer omitted information from machine-generated messages, as they commonly do in human communication, and whether such pragmatic communication improves assistance in dynamic monitoring tasks.
AI.method: The authors conducted a preregistered monitoring-task study with 114 participants. They manipulated participants’ prior knowledge and the time available to detect critical situations. Participants interacted with either a pragmatic planner, which modeled the user’s knowledge and selected what to say, when to say it, and how explicitly to phrase it, or a baseline system that reported problems fully and in onset order. Performance, response speed, problem detection, helpfulness ratings, and reported mental demand were compared across conditions.
AI.result: Participants interpreted underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified alerts, responded sooner, and detected more problems with the pragmatic assistant. They also rated the pragmatic system as helpful more frequently. These benefits did not come with an increase in self-reported mental demand.
AI.conclusion: People can reconstruct information that an assistive system leaves implicit when their prior knowledge supports the inference. Knowledge-aware pragmatic communication can therefore make assistance more efficient and effective in rapidly changing environments by reducing unnecessary information while preserving comprehension.

title: Agentic Path Maps: Exposing an Agent's Traversal Through the Garden of Forking Paths
summary: When an AI agent executes an underspecified task, it embeds choices that may contradict unarticulated user context and preferences. However, interrupting the user for clarification on all such decisions is untenable. How might agents communicate impactful, but unexplored, paths to the user after execution? To investigate, we first distill a design space for communicating alternative paths, supporting the generation of new systems and structuring dimensions of future study. We then measure the impact of one vital design space dimension on user comprehension: the number of alternatives displayed. Through a user study (n=48) in the data analysis domain, we find that participants rarely consider alternative paths of their own volition, but AI overreliance reduces when alternative paths are visualized for them. By revealing paths the agent did not take, we demonstrate how users can better interpret results and incorporate personal context.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how AI agents can communicate meaningful alternative execution paths after completing underspecified tasks. It proposes a design space for presenting alternatives and empirically examines how the number of alternatives affects user comprehension. In a data-analysis study with 48 participants, visualizing alternatives reduced AI overreliance and helped users incorporate personal context.
AI.motivation: AI agents must often act despite incomplete instructions, making choices that may conflict with users' unstated preferences. Asking users to clarify every ambiguity is impractical, while hiding unchosen possibilities can encourage overreliance on the agent's output. The paper therefore investigates how agents can reveal impactful alternative paths after execution so users can better understand and critically evaluate results.
AI.method: The authors first distill a design space for communicating alternative execution paths, intended to guide the design of future systems and research. They then conduct a user study with 48 participants in a data-analysis setting, focusing on the effect of one design dimension: the number of alternatives displayed. Participants' consideration of alternatives, comprehension of results, and reliance on AI outputs are evaluated.
AI.result: Participants rarely generated or considered alternative paths without assistance. When the AI visualized alternatives, participants showed reduced overreliance on the AI and were better able to interpret the results and account for their own contextual preferences. The abstract does not specify the comparative effect of displaying different numbers of alternatives in detail.
AI.conclusion: Presenting unchosen but impactful execution paths can make AI behavior more transparent and support more appropriate user judgment. Rather than interrupting users before every ambiguous decision, agents can communicate alternatives after execution, helping users detect context-sensitive issues and avoid blind reliance on AI outputs.

title: OmniScribble: Mixed-Initiative Authoring of Animated Sketches through Inspectable and Repairable AI Decisions
summary: AI-assisted creative tools reduce the effort of authoring content, but delegating creative decisions to AI can make it difficult for authors to understand, correct, or redirect work. We present OmniScribble, a system for animating multi-object sketches that treats object decomposition and motion planning as editable artifacts. Rather than generating animation end-to-end, OmniScribble presents AI proposals at verification checkpoints, where authors can accept, repair, or regenerate them. Both manual and AI-assisted authoring operate on the intermediate representation and rendering pipeline, allowing us to isolate AI delegation. In a within-subject study with eight participants, AI-assisted authoring yielded a median within-participant reduction in completion time of 71.4\%, while perceived control and motion-intent alignment remained high. Interaction traces and interviews show that participants adapted to AI errors by repairing local issues, regenerating mismatches, and accepting proposals. These findings suggest that inspectable, repairable delegation enables generative automation while maintaining control over the outcome.

AI.tldr: OmniScribble is an AI-assisted system for animating multi-object sketches that exposes object decomposition and motion planning as editable intermediate artifacts. A within-subject study with eight participants found a 71.4% median reduction in completion time while preserving perceived control and alignment with motion intent.
AI.motivation: End-to-end AI generation can reduce authoring effort but may obscure creative decisions and make errors difficult to understand, correct, or redirect. The paper investigates whether inspectable and repairable AI delegation can provide automation without sacrificing author control.
AI.method: The system generates proposals at verification checkpoints rather than producing animation end-to-end. Object decomposition and motion plans are represented as editable artifacts, and users can accept, locally repair, or regenerate proposals. Manual and AI-assisted workflows share the same intermediate representation and rendering pipeline, enabling a controlled comparison. A within-subject study with eight participants, supplemented by interaction-trace analysis and interviews, evaluated efficiency, perceived control, and motion-intent alignment.
AI.result: AI assistance produced a median within-participant completion-time reduction of 71.4%. Participants maintained high perceived control and strong alignment between generated motion and intended motion. They handled errors through a combination of local repair, regeneration, and acceptance, adapting their behavior to the type of mismatch.
AI.conclusion: Inspectable, repairable delegation can combine generative automation with authorial control. Treating AI outputs as editable intermediate artifacts, and exposing them at verification checkpoints, supports efficient creative authoring while preserving the ability to understand and redirect results.

title: SEAM: Situated Executable Associative Memory for a Co-located Community
summary: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.

AI.tldr: SEAM is a social-app prototype that creates a shared, associative, and programmable memory for communities. In a two-week deployment with 46 people and a follow-up workshop with 14, participants used it to share experiences, query collective knowledge, track routines, play games, and discover unfamiliar people and topics. The study suggests a model in which community knowledge can proactively reach relevant members.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the problem of fragmented knowledge in groups. Although individuals possess complementary information, its integration depends on social relationships and may fail to reach people who could benefit from it. The authors seek to design a community-scale memory system inspired by human recall, including contextual association, situated responses, and member-driven adaptation.
AI.method: The authors designed and prototyped SEAM, a social application in which members post arbitrary moments. The system identifies relationships among these fragments, synthesizes group-level knowledge, and responds associatively to queries or situations. Some user contributions function as instructions that modify system behavior, making the shared memory programmable. They evaluated SEAM through a two-week open-ended deployment with 46 co-located community members, followed by a workshop involving 14 participants.
AI.result: Participants used SEAM to document daily experiences, query the shared memory, instruct it to monitor routines, and create games. The system also generated responses that connected members with people and topics they had not previously encountered. These observations indicate that associative retrieval and programmable community rules can support both knowledge sharing and social discovery, although the abstract does not report quantitative performance measures or controlled comparisons.
AI.conclusion: SEAM demonstrates a promising direction for community knowledge systems in which information is not merely stored for later retrieval but actively finds relevant people. The work suggests that shared memory can combine collective knowledge integration, contextual interaction, and user-programmable behavior, while the exploratory evaluation provides initial evidence rather than definitive causal validation.

title: From Watching to Steering: Enabling Human-Coding Agent Collaboration through Execution Traces
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled coding agents to autonomously perform complex software development tasks, yet their long-running execution remains difficult for users to inspect, understand, and steer. We present Vibetrace, an interactive trace visualization and intervention system for agentic programming built upon OpenCode. Vibetrace introduces a human-agent collaboration paradigm of Observe, Understand, Intervene, and Evolve. It (1) visualizes agent workflows as interactive execution traces for inspecting actions, intermediate states, and failures; (2) enables users to fork execution from prior steps and provide targeted corrections without restarting validated progress; and (3) distills traces and human feedback into reusable skills for continual agent evolution. On SWE-bench Verified, distilled skills reduce input tokens by 23.0% and cost by 15.5%, while improving pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0%. User studies further demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional log-based interaction.

AI.tldr: Vibetrace is an interactive visualization and intervention system for long-running coding agents. It makes agent execution inspectable, allows users to correct and fork from earlier states, and converts interaction traces into reusable skills. On SWE-bench Verified, it reduces tokens and cost while modestly improving task success, and user studies show better accuracy and efficiency than log-based interaction.
AI.motivation: Coding agents powered by large language models can handle complex software tasks, but their long-running behavior is difficult for users to inspect, understand, and control. Conventional logs provide limited support for diagnosing failures or correcting an agent without discarding useful progress. The paper addresses the need for a more transparent, steerable, and continually improving human-agent collaboration workflow.
AI.method: The paper presents Vibetrace, built on OpenCode, using an Observe–Understand–Intervene–Evolve paradigm. It represents agent behavior as interactive execution traces containing actions, intermediate states, and failures; supports forking execution from previous steps so users can apply targeted corrections while preserving validated work; and distills execution traces plus human feedback into reusable skills for future agent runs. The system is evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and through user studies against conventional log-based interaction.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, distilled skills reduce input-token usage by 23.0% and cost by 15.5%, while increasing the pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0%. User studies report improved accuracy and efficiency compared with conventional log-based interaction. The abstract does not provide sample sizes, statistical significance, or detailed task-level results.
AI.conclusion: Interactive trace visualization, non-destructive intervention, and skill distillation can make coding agents more transparent, controllable, efficient, and capable of continual improvement. Vibetrace demonstrates that human feedback is more valuable when integrated directly into the execution trace and reused across future tasks. The evidence is promising, though the abstract alone does not establish the system’s generalizability beyond the reported benchmark and user-study settings.

title: Setting the Stage: Enhancing Music Recommendations with Spoken Introductions to Stimulate Serendipity
summary: People like to keep their music listening fresh and interesting, but recommender systems often struggle to support this need. Even when a recommended song is potentially refreshing and enriching, listeners may not perceive it as such. Building on Silvia's appraisal theory of interest, this paper studies whether enhancing recommendations with spoken introductions, immersive or informative, can stimulate two distinct flavors of experienced serendipity: taste-broadening (sparking interest in music outside one's typical preferences) and taste-deepening (deepening interest in music within one's typical preferences). Results from a large-scale user study show that both introduction types stimulate taste-broadening and taste-deepening serendipity. Taste-broadening is most effectively stimulated through transportation (absorption in a narrative world), whereas taste-deepening is most effectively stimulated through cognitive elaboration (learning something new about the artist or the social context in which the music emerged). We discuss how these findings could be translated into practice through curated taste-broadening playlists, where both introduction types appear promising, and taste-deepening playlists, where informative introductions seem particularly effective.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how spoken introductions accompanying music recommendations can foster two forms of experienced serendipity: taste-broadening and taste-deepening. Both immersive and informative introductions are effective, but through different mechanisms: immersive introductions promote transportation and broader musical exploration, while informative introductions promote cognitive elaboration and deeper engagement with familiar musical preferences.
AI.motivation: Music recommender systems may identify novel or valuable songs, yet users do not always experience these recommendations as refreshing or serendipitous. The paper addresses this perception gap by investigating whether spoken contextual introductions can make recommendations more engaging and support two distinct outcomes: discovering music beyond existing tastes and developing deeper appreciation within those tastes.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale user study comparing two types of spoken introductions to recommended songs: immersive introductions designed to draw listeners into a narrative world, and informative introductions designed to provide knowledge about the artist or the social context of the music. Drawing on Silvia’s appraisal theory of interest, the study examined whether these introductions stimulated taste-broadening and taste-deepening serendipity, and whether transportation or cognitive elaboration explained the effects.
AI.result: Both immersive and informative introductions stimulated both taste-broadening and taste-deepening serendipity. Taste-broadening was most strongly associated with transportation, or absorption in the narrative world. Taste-deepening was most strongly associated with cognitive elaboration, particularly learning new information about the artist or the music’s social context.
AI.conclusion: Spoken introductions can enhance the experienced serendipity of music recommendations, although different introduction styles are better suited to different goals. Both styles are promising for curated taste-broadening playlists, while informative introductions appear especially suitable for taste-deepening playlists.

title: Making Smell Actionable in Design: Lexicon, Movement Patterns, and Gesture Cards
summary: Smell is powerful in design, yet it often remains vague and difficult to work with in studios and classrooms. While olfactory HCI has produced devices, toolkits, and scenario-based applications, designers still lack teachable, shareable resources that link smell to bodily action. This paper presents a three-phase research program that makes smell actionable by moving from lived smell experiences to movement patterns and, finally, to gesture resources. We study olfactory-motor mappings and package the results as teachable design representations through a progressively narrowing method: (1) extracting smell-verb-intent relations from user narratives; (2) capturing and clustering embodied enactments into standardized upper-limb trajectory families; and (3) translating these trajectories into gesture card representations for design teaching and ideation through design workshops. We present a three-phase translational framework and empirically derived smell-gesture correspondences that structure the smell-intent-trajectory-gesture pathway, together with reusable assets (lexicon, trajectory atlas, gesture tables, and cards) that support teaching, reuse, and adaptation across contexts.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a three-phase framework for transforming subjective smell experiences into teachable, reusable gesture resources for olfactory interaction design. It links smell, intention, bodily movement, and gesture representations through narrative analysis, motion capture and clustering, and design workshops.
AI.motivation: Smell is influential in design but remains difficult to articulate, standardize, and teach. Existing olfactory HCI research provides technologies and applications, yet designers lack practical resources that connect olfactory experience with bodily action and support ideation, communication, and reuse across design contexts.
AI.method: The study uses a progressively narrowing three-phase translational method. First, user narratives are analyzed to extract relationships among smells, action-oriented verbs, and intentions. Second, embodied enactments are captured and clustered into standardized upper-limb movement trajectory families. Third, the trajectories are converted into gesture cards and related design representations, which are evaluated and refined through design workshops. The resulting resource set includes a smell lexicon, trajectory atlas, gesture tables, and gesture cards.
AI.result: The paper produces a three-phase translational framework and empirically derived correspondences between smell, intention, movement trajectory, and gesture. It also delivers reusable teaching and ideation assets intended to make olfactory experiences more actionable, communicable, and adaptable.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a structured pathway from lived smell experience to embodied movement and finally to design-oriented gesture resources. By externalizing olfactory-motor mappings into reusable representations, it contributes a practical foundation for teaching and designing smell-based interactions, while also enabling comparison, adaptation, and further research across contexts.

title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
comment: Accepted in 25th International Conference on Mobile and Ubiquitous Multimedia (MUM) 2026
summary: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges. We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel. One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a wearable-mediated channel for discreet social-robot communication, combining private in-ear audio with intentional rightward head tilts. In a Wizard-of-Oz card-game study with 40 participants, the channel functioned reliably and was usable, but participants differed in whether the covert exchange was noticed and whether it felt collaborative or unfair.
AI.motivation: Public speech and visible gestures can expose information to bystanders in shared environments. The study addresses the need for interaction mechanisms that allow a social robot to communicate selectively with one person while limiting others’ access to or interpretation of the exchange. It also examines social and ethical concerns, particularly awareness, perceived teamwork, and fairness.
AI.method: The researchers conducted a within-pair comparison with 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent operated through a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played both with and without the wearable channel. One participant received private in-ear messages and responded through deliberate rightward head tilts; the other participant was the non-wearer and learned about the channel after gameplay. The channel transmitted information intended to help the wearer or robot character choose an opponent they could defeat. Measures included task success, perceived pressure/tension, immediate usability, and retrospective interview accounts.
AI.result: The intended information exchange and opponent selection occurred in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns, indicating high operational feasibility. Wearers reported low pressure or tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between them, and rated the channel favorably for usability. Interviews showed that non-wearers varied in whether they noticed the interaction and held contrasting views of it as either teamwork or unfair assistance.
AI.conclusion: The wearable channel is feasible for discreet robot-mediated communication in the studied card-game context and does not appear to increase users’ perceived pressure. However, successful deployment requires careful attention to how detectable the interaction is and how covert assistance affects perceptions of fairness and collaboration. The findings are promising but context-specific and should be validated in more naturalistic settings, with larger and more diverse samples and additional interaction tasks.

title: AI for eGovernance: Leveraging Language Technologies For Digital Inclusion
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Presented at AAIAC 2026, Dar es Salaam, Tanzania
summary: The Kenyan government has invested heavily in the digitisation of public service delivery, in line with the Kenya Digital Master Plan 2022-2032. The national eGovernment platform, eCitizen, hosts services that are vital to citizens' livelihoods, including business registration, youth enterprise lending, digital literacy and tax filing. However, the platform faces digital inclusion challenges that limit equitable access for marginalised groups, particularly youth in rural areas and persons with disabilities. This exclusion is driven by a language barrier, since the platform is primarily in English with limited Swahili support, and by a text-only interface that excludes low-literacy and visually impaired users. This paper reports findings from six one-on-one interviews and an eleven-person roundtable discussion across four platforms essential to youth livelihoods: Ajira Digital, Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) iTax, Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) and the Youth Enterprise Development Fund (YEDF). Drawing on these findings, on Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 principles as a design lens for diagnosing eCitizen's accessibility gaps, and on comparator models such as Estonia's Bürokratt and India's Bhashini, the paper proposes a human-centred, systems-minded framework for embedding generative AI and language technologies into eCitizen, including text simplification, neural machine translation, text-to-speech and speech-to-text. The paper argues that, when deployed responsibly with appropriate human oversight, these interventions could meaningfully improve access to government services for linguistically excluded citizens. It also emphasises that AI alone cannot overcome the broader structural barriers, including unemployment and educational inequality, that shape digital exclusion.

AI.tldr: The paper examines digital exclusion in Kenya’s eCitizen platform and proposes a responsible, human-centred framework using generative AI and language technologies to improve accessibility for rural youth, low-literacy users, and persons with disabilities.
AI.motivation: Although Kenya has invested substantially in digital public services, eCitizen remains difficult to access equitably because of limited Swahili support and a predominantly text-based interface. These barriers may prevent linguistically excluded, low-literacy, rural, and visually impaired users from accessing livelihood-related services.
AI.method: The study uses qualitative evidence from six individual interviews and an eleven-person roundtable covering Ajira Digital, KRA iTax, HELB, and YEDF. It diagnoses accessibility gaps using WCAG 2.1 as a design lens and compares relevant approaches from Estonia’s Bürokratt and India’s Bhashini. Based on these inputs, it develops a human-centred, systems-oriented framework involving text simplification, neural machine translation, text-to-speech, and speech-to-text.
AI.result: The analysis identifies language and interface design as major accessibility barriers and argues that responsibly deployed AI could improve interaction with eCitizen services. Human oversight is presented as necessary for reliable and appropriate implementation. The paper also finds that technological interventions cannot independently resolve structural causes of exclusion, such as unemployment and educational inequality.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI and language technologies could make Kenyan digital public services more inclusive, particularly when combined with accessibility standards, multilingual design, speech interfaces, and human oversight. However, AI should be treated as one component of a broader inclusion strategy rather than a standalone solution.

title: For You, Not for Everyone: Bystander-Aware Delivery of Critical Feedback in Robot Tutoring
summary: Robots in shared settings may expose information intended for an individual user to nearby bystanders. Robot tutoring makes this concern particularly salient: critical feedback is directed at an individual learner, yet bystanders may overhear or see it. To address this, we compared context-invariant and context-adaptive robot behaviors in a between-subjects study with 40 participants. Following an initial phase without a bystander, a bystander entered the setting. Participants then received two scripted critical feedback messages concerning their pronunciation and handwriting, independent of their actual performance. With the context-invariant behavior, the robot tutor delivered both messages aloud. With the context-adaptive behavior, the robot tutor scanned for the bystander, turned its body and display away after detecting them, gave a spoken attention cue, and presented the same feedback messages silently on its display. Participants rated the robot tutor higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence in the context-adaptive condition than in the context-invariant condition, while evidence for reduced experienced embarrassment was inconclusive. These findings inform the design and evaluation of robots that respond to bystander presence by adapting how they communicate potentially sensitive information.

AI.tldr: A between-subjects study with 40 participants found that a robot tutor that detects a bystander and switches from spoken to private, display-based feedback is perceived as more privacy-aware and socially competent than a robot that continues speaking aloud. Evidence that this adaptation reduces embarrassment was inconclusive.
AI.motivation: Robots used in shared environments can unintentionally disclose information intended for one person to nearby bystanders. This issue is especially important in tutoring, where critical feedback about an individual learner may be overheard or observed. The paper addresses the need for robot behaviors that protect privacy when bystanders are present.
AI.method: The authors conducted a between-subjects study with 40 participants. After an initial tutoring phase without a bystander, a bystander entered. Participants received two scripted critical feedback messages about pronunciation and handwriting, regardless of actual performance. In the context-invariant condition, the robot delivered the feedback aloud. In the context-adaptive condition, it detected the bystander, turned its body and display away, issued a spoken attention cue, and showed the feedback silently on its display. Participants evaluated privacy awareness, social competence, and experienced embarrassment.
AI.result: Participants rated the context-adaptive robot significantly or comparatively higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence than the context-invariant robot. The evidence that adaptive behavior reduced participants’ experienced embarrassment was inconclusive.
AI.conclusion: Adapting communication modality and orientation in response to bystander presence can improve perceptions of a robot tutor’s privacy awareness and social competence. The findings support designing robots that detect contextual privacy risks and communicate sensitive information discreetly, while further research is needed to establish whether such adaptations reliably reduce embarrassment.

title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
comment: 7 pages, 3 tables. Dataset and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23901549
summary: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether an LLM-based severe-weather preparedness assistant gives false reassurance when it lacks access to official NWS alerts. Across 117 replayed cases and five pipeline conditions, access to real-time alerts eliminated observed false reassurance, while prompt-based disclosure of the model’s blind spot did not. The study also identifies substantial false alarms, ingestion of test products as real alerts, and token-budget failures, and releases its data and code.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by a safety-critical failure mode: an assistant that cannot access official severe-weather alerts may incorrectly imply that conditions are safe while a warning is active. It aims to measure this false reassurance rigorously, compare alert-access and prompt-design strategies, assess whether disclosure of limitations improves safety, and identify additional operational weaknesses.
AI.method: The authors replayed 117 frozen cases derived from real U.S. National Weather Service alerts: 69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, and 16 non-U.S. cases. These were evaluated under five Claude-based preparedness-pipeline conditions varying alert access and prompt design. One rater labeled all 342 alert-case responses using a seven-category scheme developed after an initial binary pass. The study used paired statistical comparisons, confidence intervals, a preregistered single-sentence prompt ablation, and an automated regex measure that was evaluated but rejected because of poor sensitivity. It also examined ingestion of NWS test products and failures caused by limited token budgets.
AI.result: False reassurance occurred in 0/66 production-pipeline cases (0.0%; 95% CI 0.0–5.5%) and 0/69 cases with alerts under a neutral prompt, compared with 26/69 (37.7%) for a blind neutral prompt and 31/69 (44.9%) when the blind prompt additionally instructed the model to disclose its blind spot. All observed failures were implicit rather than explicit denials of an alert. Real alert access significantly reduced false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001), whereas the disclosure instruction had no significant effect (p = 0.40). Under a neutral prompt, the model raised some alarm in 87.5% of no-alert controls, versus 0% with the production prompt. The regex metric missed 53 of 57 manually identified cases. Additional failures involved treating NWS test products as real alerts and exhausting the token budget on complex cases.
AI.conclusion: Reliable access to official alert data was substantially more effective than merely instructing the model to disclose its lack of alert access. However, alert data alone did not guarantee safe behavior: prompt design strongly influenced false alarms, and system engineering issues created additional risks. The paper supports evaluating safety-critical LLM systems with frozen real-world cases, human labeling, explicit controls, and operational failure analysis rather than relying on automated surface-pattern metrics alone.

title: Whose Guardrail? User Identity Shapes the Effectiveness of Model Disclaimers in Mitigating LLM Political Persuasion
summary: Politically biased AI can shift users' opinions, yet it remains unclear whether model disclaimers protect against such persuasion. We report a preregistered experiment (N=1,586) examining how disclaimer design and user characteristics shape susceptibility to politically biased AI. We varied whether disclaimers identified political bias versus potential inaccuracies and whether they included an explanation. Participants completed two decision-making tasks with an LLM biased against their political views, with outcomes assessed immediately and one week later. Disclaimers identifying political bias and including an explanation reduced persuasion, but effects varied across contexts and did not persist. Individual differences were more consistent predictors: Republicans were more persuaded and reported higher trust than Democrats across tasks. Similarly, participants who used AI more frequently were also more persuaded, whereas those with greater self-reported AI knowledge were less persuaded. These findings suggest that generic disclaimers are not enough: effective safeguards must account for user heterogeneity and context.

AI.tldr: A preregistered experiment with 1,586 participants tested whether disclaimer wording and user characteristics moderate persuasion by politically biased AI. Disclaimers that explicitly identified political bias and explained it reduced persuasion somewhat, but effects depended on context and disappeared after one week. User characteristics—political affiliation, AI-use frequency, and AI knowledge—were more consistent predictors of susceptibility.
AI.motivation: The study addresses whether disclaimers can protect users from persuasion by politically biased AI, an important question because simply warning users about AI limitations may not prevent attitude change. It also examines whether disclaimer effectiveness varies by user characteristics and decision-making context.
AI.method: The authors conducted a preregistered experiment with N=1,586 participants. Participants completed two decision-making tasks involving an LLM that was biased against their political views. The study manipulated disclaimer type: warnings about political bias versus potential inaccuracies, and warnings with versus without an explanatory rationale. Persuasion and trust were measured immediately and again one week later, alongside individual differences such as political affiliation, AI-use frequency, and self-reported AI knowledge.
AI.result: Disclaimers that explicitly identified political bias and included an explanation reduced immediate persuasion more effectively than less specific warnings, but the effects varied by task and did not persist after one week. Individual differences were more robust: Republicans were more persuaded and reported greater trust than Democrats across tasks; frequent AI users were more susceptible, while participants with greater AI knowledge were less susceptible.
AI.conclusion: Generic disclaimers are insufficient as a durable safeguard against politically biased AI persuasion. Effective interventions should explicitly communicate the type and source of bias, provide explanations, and be tailored to user characteristics and context. The findings also indicate that short-term reductions in persuasion may not translate into lasting protection.
